newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kremlin takes hard line on NATO ahead Kohl talks.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin takes hard line on NATO ahead Kohl talks.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman warned on Wednesday that Russia might refuse to sign a planned treaty with NATO if it failed to meet Moscow's security concerns.

Sounding a hard line on the eve of Yeltsin's talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news conference any treaty must be binding and take account of Russia's wish to limit the change in military deployments after east European states join the bloc.
"If the treaty is not binding and concrete on military matters there would scarcely be any point for Russia in signing such a document," Yastrzhembsky said.

After talks on Tuesday between Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, officials said there was broad agreement but difficulties remained over Russia's insistence on keeping NATO troops and weapons behind present frontiers.
Yastrzhembsky said it would be "premature" to say what the chances were of signing a Russia-NATO treaty in Paris at the end of May. Primakov said last week he hoped a treaty could be ready by then.

Maintaining Moscow's harsh criticism of NATO's plans, Yastrzhembsky said that, treaty or no treaty, Moscow would not change its opinion that expanding NATO eastward was "the West's greatest historic mistake since the end of the Cold War".

"For us it is an absolute priority that the document which is now being worked out has a binding character for all those who sign it. For us it is especially important that this document has the most concrete possible formulas on military issues," Yastrzhembsky said.

Agreement at the Paris meeting would set the stage for a July NATO summit in Madrid at which the defence alliance is expected to invite several former Communist Warsaw Pact countries to start negotiations on full NATO membership.
The first wave of nations asked to join the alliance's eastward expansion is expected to be made up of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Yastrzhemsky said that among the points Yeltsin would raise with Kohl would be to brief Kohl on the result of his Helsinki summit with Clinton and on the subsequent developments.
Yeltsin also wanted to discuss increasing the role of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which Russia sees as a less partisan body than NATO.
Yastrzhemsky said they hoped Kohl would be able to help them reach a compromise in negotiations with NATO.

He said they also discussed preparations for the G7 plus Russia in Denver in the United States in the summer and were counting on a continuation of German support for Russia's increased role in this body.
